html:
The Kushan kings, who ruled from Bactria to the Ganges plain, began striking gold coins on a large scale around 100 CE. Vima Kadphises started it, and Kanishka and his successors kept it up. Much of the gold probably came from Roman coins paid for Indian goods, melted and restruck; the Kushan gold coin matched the weight of the Roman aureus.

The coins show the king in nomad dress, long coat, trousers and boots, often making an offering at a fire altar. On the back is one of many gods: Iranian gods of the moon, sun and fire, Greek Helios, Oesho (often linked with Shiva), and under Kanishka one of the earliest images of the Buddha, labelled BODDO. Their legends moved from Greek to the Bactrian language written in Greek letters.

The coins are a main source for the Kushans' religions and for their trade with the Roman Empire by sea and along the Silk Road. Later the Gupta kings of India based their own gold coins on the Kushan standard.
